title: The Beekeeper of Sorrows
summary: In the hills above Honeydown lives an old woman whose bees gather sorrow instead of pollen. When Wrenna asks to have her grief taken away for good, she learns that a sorrow removed cleanly takes the love it was made of with it.

chapters.title: The Hives on the Hill
chapters.body:
Above the village of Honeydown, on a hill where the wildflowers grew thickest, stood a row of pale wooden beehives, and an old woman who tended them. Everyone in the valley knew her, and everyone was a little afraid of her, because her bees did not make ordinary honey.

Her bees gathered sorrow.

It worked like this: when a grief grew too heavy to carry — a loss that wouldn't lift, a sadness that sat on the chest like a stone — you climbed the hill to the beekeeper, and you sat with her among the humming hives, and you told her your sorrow. And as you spoke, her bees would come, drawn to the grief the way ordinary bees are drawn to nectar, and they would settle on you, gentle as breath, and draw the sorrow out of you sip by sip. They carried it back to the hives, and there they turned it into honey — a dark, bitter-gold honey that the beekeeper kept in rows of jars in her cottage, each labeled with a name and a date. And you would walk back down the hill lighter, the worst weight of your grief gone, able to breathe again.

The beekeeper never took it all. That was the thing people whispered about, uneasily, not quite understanding. She always left a little. However much you begged her to take the whole terrible weight, she left a small ache behind, every time, and would not explain why.

Wrenna was twelve, and she had a sorrow she wanted gone completely.

Her mother had died in the spring. And Wrenna had carried the grief through the summer, and it had not lifted — it woke her at night, it ambushed her in the middle of ordinary days, it sat on her chest so heavy some mornings she could hardly rise. She was so tired of hurting. She wanted it to stop. And so, when autumn came, she climbed the hill to the beekeeper's hives, and she asked for the one thing everyone secretly wanted and no one was ever given.

"Take all of it," Wrenna said. "Please. Not a little. All of it. I don't want to feel it anymore. I don't want to miss her anymore. It hurts too much. Take the whole thing."

The old beekeeper looked at her for a long moment, with eyes the soft gold of old honey, and there was a great gentleness in her face, and a great sadness too.

"I can do that, child," she said quietly. "I'm one of the few who can. My bees can take a grief right down to the root, and leave nothing behind — no ache, no weight, nothing. You'd walk down this hill and never hurt over your mother again." She paused. "But I never do it. And before I do it for you, you have to understand what it costs. Because everyone who begs for the whole sorrow to be taken doesn't yet know what a sorrow is made of."

chapters.title: What a Sorrow Is Made Of
chapters.body:
The beekeeper led Wrenna into her cottage, where the shelves were lined with jars of dark honey, each with its name and date, and she took one down.

"This one," she said, "belonged to a man who came to me years ago. His wife had died, and his grief was terrible, and he begged me, as you're begging me now, to take all of it. And I was younger then, and I hadn't yet learned, and so I did. I sent my bees to take the whole sorrow, down to the root." She turned the jar in the light. "And it worked. He walked down the hill and never grieved his wife again. Never wept for her. Never ached." She set the jar down. "But here is what I didn't understand, and what he didn't understand. A sorrow is not a separate thing that lands on you from outside. A sorrow is made of love. It is the shape your love takes when the person you love is gone. The grief and the love are the same thing, child — the missing is just the loving, with nowhere left to go."

Wrenna frowned. "So?"

"So when I took his whole sorrow," the beekeeper said, "I took the love it was made of. He walked down the hill and never grieved his wife — because he could no longer remember loving her. Oh, he remembered the facts. He knew he'd had a wife, knew her name, knew she'd died. But the feeling was gone, all of it, because I'd drawn it out with the grief, right down to the root. He would look at her picture and feel nothing. He would hear her favorite song and feel nothing. The bees had taken the pain, yes — but the pain was just the love hurting, and once it was gone, the love was gone with it. He'd traded away the ache of missing her, and paid with every warm thing he'd ever felt for her. He didn't grieve her anymore. He just... didn't have her anymore, not even inside himself. And that, he told me at the end of his life, was far worse. He said he'd give anything to hurt over her again, because at least the hurting had been full of her."

Wrenna was quiet, holding the dark jar, thinking of her mother.

"That," said the beekeeper, "is why I always leave a little. The small ache I leave behind isn't cruelty, child. It's the love. It's the part of your grief that is really just how much you loved them, kept safe, so that you get to keep loving them even though they're gone. I take enough to let you breathe, to let you live, to lift the weight that would crush you. But I leave the root — the tender part, the part that aches when you remember them — because that ache is the last way you have of holding them. Take that away, and you don't heal. You just lose them twice."

Wrenna looked at the jar, and then out the window at the hives humming on the hill, and she thought about what she had climbed up here to ask for. She had wanted the missing to stop. She had thought the missing was the enemy. But the beekeeper was telling her that the missing was the love — that to stop missing her mother completely would mean forgetting how it felt to love her at all.

chapters.title: The Ache Worth Keeping
chapters.body:
Wrenna sat among the hives for a long time, and the bees hummed around her, and she thought about her mother.

She thought about the weight that woke her at night, the stone on her chest, the grief that ambushed her in ordinary moments. She still wanted that gone — the crushing part, the part that made it hard to breathe and hard to live. She was still a child, and no child should have to carry a full-grown grief through every hour of every day.

But she thought, too, about the man in the jar, who had traded the ache for emptiness and found the emptiness far worse. Who had given anything, at the end, to hurt over his wife again — because the hurting had at least been full of her. And Wrenna understood, at last, what the beekeeper had been trying to teach her. There is a difference between a grief that crushes you and a grief that connects you. The first you cannot live under. The second you would not want to live without.

"Take the weight," Wrenna said finally. "The part that wakes me at night. The part that's too heavy. I can't carry all of it — I'm not big enough yet." She swallowed. "But leave the rest. Leave the part that... that aches when I remember her. The part that misses her. I understand now. That part is her. That part is me loving her. I don't want to lose that. Even though it hurts. Especially because it hurts."

The old beekeeper smiled, and it was the smile of someone who has waited a long time to hear a child say a wise thing.

"Then you already understand more than most grown men ever do," she said softly. "Sit still, child. And think of her while my bees work. Think of the good — the weight will lift, but the thinking-of-her will stay."

And the bees came. Gentle as breath, they settled on Wrenna's shoulders and her hair and her folded hands, and she felt them begin to draw the sorrow out of her — but only the crushing part, only the stone. As they worked, Wrenna did as she was told: she thought of her mother. She thought of her mother's hands braiding her hair, and her mother's laugh, and the song her mother used to hum while cooking, and the way her mother said her name. And with each memory, she felt the terrible weight lift, sip by sip — but the warmth stayed. The love stayed. When she remembered her mother's laugh, it still brought a small sweet ache, a missing that was really just loving — and the bees left that untouched, because that was the root, and the root was never theirs to take.

When it was done, Wrenna stood, and she could breathe. The stone was gone from her chest. The grief no longer crushed her. She could live again, could sleep again, could walk down the hill into the rest of her childhood without a full-grown sorrow dragging at every step.

But when she thought of her mother — and she did, every day, for the rest of her life — there was still that small tender ache. The good ache. The one that meant I loved you, and I remember, and you are still here, in the only place you can be. And Wrenna was glad of it, every time, even when it brought tears. Because she had learned the thing the man in the jar had learned too late: that the ache of missing someone is not a wound to be cured. It is love, still burning, for someone the world took away. And that is a fire worth tending, no matter how it stings.

The beekeeper watched the girl walk back down the hill, lighter but not emptied, healed but not hollowed, and she nodded to herself, and went back to her hives. And she never took a whole sorrow again for anyone — but she never had to explain why, to Wrenna. Because some children, when you tell them what a sorrow is truly made of, understand at once that the missing and the loving are the same thing, and that you must never, ever let anyone take all of it away.
